article_sentences: A 4.2 magnitude earthquake struck Uttarakhand's Uttarkashi district on Saturday night (October 10, 2026), sending strong tremors across the Uttarkashi town and the Yamunotri valley.
According to the National Centre for Seismology, the earthquake, measuring 4.2, struck at 8.07 p.m., with its epicentre located two km northwest of Uttarkashi at a depth of 11 km.
Purushottam Uniyal, a priest from Kharsali village, the winter seat of Yamunotri, said the tremors were strong enough to cause televisions inside homes to shake.
The sudden and intense tremors triggered panic, prompting people to rush outdoors, he said.
Saturday's earthquake was the second tremor measuring above 4.0 on to hit Uttarakhand in four days.
A 4.9-magnitude earthquake had struck Chamoli district on October 6.
Officials of the Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) said no damage had been reported so far.

stories.headline: The legacy of a studio that captured a century in image
stories.title: The legacy of a studio that captured a century in image
stories.summary: “I recall feeling a profound sense of anticipation when I captured the quintessential aerial shot at a Reliance refinery nearly a decade ago. In my quest for the perfect photograph, I climbed a water tank, captured the image and felt a deep sense of satisfaction. I was unaware that the endeavour would turn me into a target for a swarm of bees. As I turned to climb down the tank, a swarm—or, more precisely, a storm—of bees enveloped me. I tried to flee, but all I received in return were more stings.” As Mr. Pavan Mehta showcases his remarkable collection of 900 cameras—ranging from a Yashica from the 1960s to a Rolleiflex dating back to 1905—he recounts the above incident as one of the defining moments of his photographic journey. He follows it with another story, equally compelling but deeply personal that traces the history of his family's enduring relationship with photography. Mehtas at the Maharaja’s Service Amarnath Mehta, a young man from Gurdaspur, travelled to Dalhousie, where a member of the military introduced him to the intricate craft of photography. In 1915, he began documenting Srinagar, establishing his studio on a houseboat on the Jhelum. As the studio expanded, it went on to preserve countless moments from Gulmarg and Pahalgam in Kashmir, extending its reach to Rawalpindi and Murree, now in Pakistan. Before Partition, the Mehtas held the prestigious position of official photographers to Maharaja Hari Singh, the last reigning Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir. In the early 1940s, amid the upheaval of the Second World War, authorities in Srinagar restricted the sale of photographic film to one roll per person to curb hoarding and the black market that often accompanies scarcity. A historical photograph of Europeans queuing for film remains preserved in the studio's collection. Following India's independence, Amarnath established a studio in Connaught Place in 1948, while the studio in Pakistan was eventually closed. Mr. Mehta recalls an era when family photography was a ritual woven into the fabric of everyday life—from celebrations to moments of grief. Around Diwali, families would gather to have their photographs taken and framed. Newly married couples would arrive in their finest attire, with women dressed in traditional ensembles and men in formal suits. Those who believed they had little time left would often choose to have their portraits taken, while relatives sometimes hurried to capture the final moments of a loved one's life in the hope of preserving the memory forever. With the arrival of smartphones, however, such practices have largely faded into the past. The Challenges of Smartphones and AI Although digital photography has made image-making more accessible than ever, it has also created a new challenge: preservation. While photographic negatives can survive for centuries under the right conditions, the long-term storage and organisation of millions of digital images present a different set of problems. Mr. Mehta emphasises the need for systematic cataloguing to ensure that these visual records are not lost in the digital age. For him, adapting to technological change is essential to survival. The studio has responded by publishing books and expanding into corporate, wedding, fashion and event photography, as well as food photography—areas that have helped make the business both commercially viable and sustainable. The studio's official Instagram account also carries short explainer reels featuring Mr. Arjun Mahatta, Pavan Mehta's son, who introduces viewers to a selection of vintage cameras. The initiative seeks to keep alive the enduring legacy of film photography at a time when digital technology dominates image-making. Photography as a profession, Mr. Mehta observes, is intensely competitive. Simply holding a camera, he argues, does not make one a photographer. A fundamental understanding of photography, acquired through study and practice, is essential to mastering the craft. Equally challenging is the task of developing a distinct photographic identity, particularly in an era increasingly shaped by AI-generated imagery. For aspiring photographers, Mr. Mehta offers a simple principle: “Before you shoot, see. Prior to engaging the shutter, it is essential to meticulously contemplate your composition. You observe, you anticipate, and you click.” In his view, patience, composition and an element of chance must come together to produce a photograph that approaches perfection. Asked to define photography in a single term, Mr. Pavan Mehta describes it as “art cultivated by curiosity” and a discipline in itself. “It is, quite literally, the act of creating imagery through the manipulation of light,” he says. “To achieve this, it is essential to comprehend the nature of light itself.” Drawing on Walter Benjamin's influential essay Little History of Photography, one can view photographs as visual records of existence—fragments of time preserved for future generations. It is precisely this quality that makes photographs valuable tools for remembering and interpreting history. Picturing a Century Pavan Mehta's book, Picturing a Century (1915–2015), offers a compelling illustration of this idea. The book chronicles a century of the Mahatta family's photographic journey alongside the social and political transformations of the country. Mr. Mehta points out that the family did not operate as an extension of any political party, yet its cameras documented pivotal moments in India's history, including the Kargil War and the funeral procession of Jawaharlal Nehru. Through their lenses, the photographers became observers—and chroniclers—of events as they unfolded. The story of Mahatta began with formal studio portraits captured on fragile glass-plate negatives and has since travelled through successive technological revolutions—from hand-painted photographs and film to digital imaging, selfies and, eventually, artificial intelligence. The studio has continually adapted to technological change. In 1954, it began hand-painting black-and-white photographs, carefully adding colour and detail by hand. It later became India's first authorised distributor of Kodak products. When photography moved from analogue to digital, Mahatta once again adapted, embracing India's first digital imaging system. Today, Mahatta & Co. operates from M-Block in Connaught Place, in a building leased from the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC). The family has operated its studio from the premises for generations. LIC, however, maintains that the studio is an “unauthorised occupant.” The Mahatta family disputes the claim, pointing to its longstanding presence in the building. Pavan Mahatta says the family occupied the premises even before LIC came into existence. He fears that forcing the studio to leave would mean Delhi losing an important part of its photographic heritage. The irony is difficult to miss. In the 1980s, Mahatta & Co. photographed the construction of the LIC building, designed by renowned Indian architect Charles Correa. Decades later, the studio finds itself on the other side of a dispute concerning the very premises from which it documented the city's transformation. The premises represent far more than a commercial establishment. They embody generations of the Mahatta family's photographic history in Delhi. For a studio that has spent more than a century documenting the lives, celebrations, tragedies and transformations of others, the present moment offers an unexpected turn: Mahatta & Co. has itself become part of the story it has spent generations recording. Syeda Shua Zaidi and Sadiya Tahseen are pursuing master in Convergent Journalism from AJK Mass Communication Research Centre, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi.

stories.headline: The Last Citizen
stories.title: The Last Citizen
stories.summary: The morning train from Katra reaches Srinagar a little after eleven. On the platform at Nowgam last week I watched a grandmother from Kupwara step down from it, having crossed the Chenab on a bridge higher than the Eiffel Tower, sitting, with a cup of tea, in three hours. For most of my life "I took the train to Srinagar" was a sentence nobody in the Valley could say. The line was sanctioned in 1994. Every government since owned a piece of it. This one finished it. On 7 October 2001, in Gandhinagar, a man who had never sat in a legislature took oath as Chief Minister of a state nine months out from an earthquake that had killed fourteen thousand people. Twenty-five years later he is Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, and there has not been one day in that quarter century when he was not the elected head of a government. No Indian, not Jyoti Basu, not Pawan Chamling, has been continuously answerable to voters for so long. The anniversary invites praise, and praise is the one thing he has never shown any sign of needing. It deserves instead an argument that can be tested. Here is mine. These twenty-five years are the story of the Indian state learning to reach its last citizen, first in one state and then in all of them. What travelled from Gandhinagar to Delhi was a method, not a mood: saturation targets instead of coverage ratios, technology used as an equaliser, several schemes converging on one household, deadlines reviewed in person. It is the method, more than the man, that explains the numbers. And the numbers that settle the argument are not the government's own; they are the Census, the Registrar General's and the World Bank's. Remember the country of 2001. Fifty-six households in a hundred had electricity, thirty-six a latrine, thirty-seven a tap, eighteen a gas connection. One child in fifteen died before its first birthday. A bank account was a favour, and a gas cylinder came with a politician's letter. That was the baseline. Then Gujarat. In 2003 the state separated the farm feeder from the village feeder and gave the village twenty-four-hour power; agricultural output grew at 9.6 percent a year between 2000 and 2007, by IFPRI's count, against 2.9 percent for India. The Soil Health Card was a Gujarat card before it was an Indian one. The grievance screen in the Chief Minister's office became PRAGATI. The Garib Kalyan Mela became the saturation camp every state now runs. Gujarat was the laboratory. India was the canvas. On the canvas, the household became the unit of delivery. Jan Dhan, mocked as a zero-balance gesture in 2014, holds 59 crore accounts today, more than half of them women's, and they are the rails on which every later transfer ran. A woman who has sat in those kitchens counts the cylinder in hours returned, not in connections. Ujjwala put 10.57 crore cylinders into kitchens that had cooked on wood. Rural households with a tap went from 3.23 crore in 2019 to 15.85 crore. Ayushman Bharat has paid for 13.25 crore hospital admissions. Direct transfer has removed 3.48 lakh crore rupees of leakage. The national highway network grew from 91,287 kilometres to 1,46,572; airports from 74 to 165; UPI, which did not exist in 2014, moved 314 lakh crore rupees last year. Infant mortality fell from 39 to 24 per thousand. Three crore rural women have crossed the Lakhpati Didi line. Left-wing extremism, which touched 126 districts in 2013, is confined to eleven. NITI Aayog's poverty index fell from 29 percent to 11, which is 24.82 crore people; the World Bank's three-dollar line fell from 27 percent to just over five. Neither figure is the government's own. What was the method's hardest test? I can answer that, because I live inside it. In 2001 Jammu and Kashmir recorded 4,522 terrorist incidents and 996 civilians killed. In 2025 it recorded 35 incidents and 92 deaths in all, the least violent year in more than two decades. Local recruitment into militancy, 125 young men in 2021, was seven in 2024. Stone-pelting has gone. The G20 met in Srinagar in May 2023. Since 2019, 34,260 people have been elected to panchayats and councils in a territory that for decades had almost none, and 7.85 crore visitors came to the Union Territory in the three years to 2025, against 4.76 crore in the three years to 2018, even though the Valley's own arrivals halved in 2025 after Pahalgam. The men who send killers across the Line retain the capacity: twenty-six civilians were murdered at Pahalgam in April 2025, and the answer, Operation Sindoor, came on 7 May. Normalcy here is a trend that has to be defended every year, not a settled fact. But the trend is real, and a Kashmiri who denies it forfeits the right to be believed on the rest. The rest is this. In August 2019 the Valley's communications were restricted, the internet did not fully return for eighteen months, and the leaders of the mainstream parties, three former Chief Ministers among them, were placed in preventive detention. Those were hard months, and I do not write around them. They were also the reason a change that every earlier turn in this Valley had paid for in blood passed without it. Elections followed as the Supreme Court directed; turnout was 64 percent; an elected government took office in October 2024. Statehood has not yet been restored. The Prime Minister and the Home Minister have given their word that it will be, at the appropriate time, and the Court asked for it at the earliest in December 2023. When the Assembly voted on 28 September, my party objected to a resolution that reached back to the position before 2019, not to statehood itself. I belong to the party that gave the word, and I have no doubt it will be kept; the security data in this essay is the case that the time is approaching. When it comes, let it come with the Pandits' return built into it, with houses and not only posts, and with the jobs that keep young men on the platform and off the hill. Nor should the national ledger be read without its debit side, and a member of the governing party should be the first to read it. Four crore rural households still wait for a tap, and the mission that reached 15.85 crore will be judged on the last four, which are the hardest. The labour survey still finds a quarter of the young in neither work nor training, and no government should be comfortable with that. Manipur tested the state's reach harder than anywhere else, and the peace there is still being rebuilt. The second wave of 2021 found the one shortage, oxygen, that nobody had been counting, and the state learned to count it. Demonetisation is still argued over; what nobody argues about is the digital habit it built, which became UPI. By the IMF's own tables India is third in purchasing power, within a few hundred billion dollars of fourth place in current dollars, and growing faster than every economy above it. An argument that cannot survive its objections is not an argument. This one does, because not one of them is an objection to reach, scale or speed. So what will outlast him? The rails: identity, account, payment, which no successor can switch off. The direct transfer, which made the intermediary politically expendable. The GST Council, in which the Centre holds one vote in three and almost every decision has been taken by consensus. The doctrine that an attack is answered across the Line. The three criminal codes of 2024, and a temple at Ayodhya built after a unanimous Supreme Court judgment, which are the same confidence turned inward. And one thing larger than all of these: Indians now expect their state to arrive. In 2001 a tap was a favour. In 2026 its absence is a grievance that a Collector in Nuh expects to be ranked on. That change in expectation is the structural achievement, and a people who have learned to expect delivery do not unlearn it when the deliverer changes. What must now be built into the state is the dashboard itself, so that the deadline holds when the review passes to other hands. The Prime Minister has said that the goal is a developed India by 2047, and that no one man is the goal. The next decade will show whether the method has been made the state's own, as he intends. The afternoon train leaves Srinagar at two. I went back to watch it go: students for Jammu, pilgrims, a box of apples wrapped in newspaper, a soldier asleep before the platform had cleared. The state learned, over a quarter century, to arrive. It has not yet learned to stay. That is the work of the next twenty-five years, and it belongs to everyone who will still be here when the man who taught it to arrive is not. The train is pulling out. The platform is ours. (The Author is Vice President, Bharatiya Janata Party, Jammu and Kashmir. She can be reached at: sganai19@gmail.com)

The direct transfer, which made the intermediary politically expendable.
The GST Council, in which the Centre holds one vote in three and almost every decision has been taken by consensus.
The doctrine that an attack is answered across the Line.
The three criminal codes of 2024, and a temple at Ayodhya built after a unanimous Supreme Court judgment, which are the same confidence turned inward.
And one thing larger than all of these: Indians now expect their state to arrive.
In 2001 a tap was a favour.
In 2026 its absence is a grievance that a Collector in Nuh expects to be ranked on.
That change in expectation is the structural achievement, and a people who have learned to expect delivery do not unlearn it when the deliverer changes.
What must now be built into the state is the dashboard itself, so that the deadline holds when the review passes to other hands.
The Prime Minister has said that the goal is a developed India by 2047, and that no one man is the goal.
The next decade will show whether the method has been made the state's own, as he intends.
The afternoon train leaves Srinagar at two.
I went back to watch it go: students for Jammu, pilgrims, a box of apples wrapped in newspaper, a soldier asleep before the platform had cleared.
The state learned, over a quarter century, to arrive.
It has not yet learned to stay.
That is the work of the next twenty-five years, and it belongs to everyone who will still be here when the man who taught it to arrive is not.
The train is pulling out.
The platform is ours.

stories.title: Mehbooba’s condemnation without PDP’s participation under scrutiny
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: People’s Democratic Party (PDP) President and former chief minister Mehbooba Mufti on Saturday drew parallels between restrictions imposed in New Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the communication blackout and security clampdown in Kashmir following the abrogation of Article 370. However, the absence of PDP leaders from the opposition’s street mobilisation in Delhi has raised questions about the party’s political positioning and its willingness to participate in a coordinated opposition campaign against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government. Criticising the restriction on ‘X’, Mehbooba posted: “Today’s Delhi is a chilling reminder of Kashmir after the unconstitutional abrogation of Article 370. People were locked in their homes, the internet was shut down, and an entire region was placed under siege. The BJP then brazenly claimed that nobody had protested. Today, with Delhi under siege, trains halted, and roads to Jantar Mantar sealed, they may repeat the same lie, claiming that nobody protested against Gyanesh Kumar. First crush the protest, then deny it ever happened. This is how enforced silence is passed off as consent.” While her words echoed the concerns articulated by most opposition leaders, the party’s visible participation in the protests has remained conspicuously limited. The political messaging has raised a question that the PDP has yet to answer publicly. If the restrictions in Delhi evoke such strong comparisons with Kashmir, why has that outrage not translated into PDP leaders’ visible presence at the protests? Talking to Greater Kashmir, PDP chief spokesperson Mehbooba Beg said, “In principle, every sensible citizen protests this naked onslaught of democracy. The institution of the Election Commission of India has got into disrepute. Registering protest is important, whether one does it through tweets, statements, or hits the streets.” He said that the Delhi protests are genuine as the ‘vote theft’ affects the 13.5 crore people including the women of West Bengal, the minorities, and the citizens of the entire country. The senior PDP leader said that the CEC Gyanesh Kumar should tender his resignation as he headed an institution that was once led by an honest person like T N Seshan. “CEC Gyanesh Kumar brought such an institution into disrepute and for that history will not judge him kindly,” he said. “The Indian Express’ investigation illustrated that anti-BJP voters had been deleted across the country and the protest is important as there was a small winning margin on many seats. Furthermore, the stand taken by the other two Election Commissioners has also made the issue of ‘vote theft’ clear.” Beg said that PDP’s stand against New Delhi had been clear after August 2019. “It was for the consistent stand taken by the PDP that the PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti’s mother (Gulshan Nazir) had been grilled by the Enforcement Directorate,” he said. While Mehbooba took to microblogging site ‘X’ on Saturday, all senior PDP leaders and legislators – Waheed-ur-Rehman Para, Muhammad Fayaz Mir, and Rafiq Ahmad Naik - as well as Mehbooba’s daughter, Iltija Mufti, were conspicuous by their absence from the Delhi mobilisation. Talking to Greater Kashmir, MLA Kupwara Muhammad Fayaz Mir and MLA Tral Rafiq Ahmad Naik said that no directions had been issued to them for participating in the Delhi protests. “I’m in Kupwara and, so far, I haven’t received any such direction,” Mir said. Naik said that he was the party’s foot soldier and would do whatever was asked of him by the party high command. Their participation could have lent greater weight to the PDP’s condemnation of the restrictions and demonstrated that its opposition extended beyond statements and social media posts. PDP’s non-participation in Delhi mobilisation leaves the party open to questions about the consistency of its opposition and the extent to which it is prepared to join a campaign beyond its own political platforms. PDP has continued to criticise the BJP-led Centre over the loss of J&K’s special status, restrictions on political activity, and other questions of civil liberties. While Mehbooba’s latest remarks reinforce the PDP’s confrontational public posture towards the Centre, the party’s absence from the Delhi protests raises questions about whether it is seeking to avoid antagonising Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) government while keeping its options open with the Congress and the wider INDIA bloc. The political metaphor of “running with the hare and hunting with the hounds” captures the suspicion surrounding this approach, as it has been denouncing the Centre’s actions but is avoiding an unambiguous demonstration of solidarity with those challenging it on the streets. PDP cannot entirely avoid scrutiny by invoking those complexities. If it believes the restrictions represent an assault on democratic freedoms, PDP leaders must explain whether they consider participation in a common opposition campaign necessary, and if not, why. Silence on that question risks allowing its opponents to portray the party’s position as selective. For Mehbooba, the immediate challenge is to reconcile the force of her public condemnation with the absence of her party’s prominent faces from the streets. The PDP’s statement may have strengthened the opposition’s argument about the curtailment of dissent. However, its absence has opened a different debate – one about whether the PDP is prepared to match its rhetoric with participation. Until the party clarifies that position, the contrast between Mehbooba’s words and her party’s political presence is likely to remain a source of scrutiny for the PDP.

stories.title: AIHCEF felicitates new Chief Justice
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: A delegation of the All India High Court Employees Federation (AIHCEF), led by its Secretary General, Asif Iqbal Mahajan, on Friday felicitated Dr Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati on assuming office as Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. It also emphasised the important role played by High Court employees in the effective functioning of the institution and expressed hope that their dedication and contributions would continue to receive due recognition. The Federation wished the Chief Justice a successful tenure, expressing hope that his leadership would further strengthen the institution’s traditions and foster an atmosphere of dignity, mutual respect and collective commitment.

stories.headline: High Court extends OPS benefit to employees appointed against posts notified before Dec 24, 2009
stories.title: High Court extends OPS benefit to employees appointed against posts notified before Dec 24, 2009
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has extended the benefit of the Old Pension Scheme (OPS) to the District Judiciary employees appointed against the posts advertised or notified prior to December 24, 2009, but subsequently joined service under the New Pension Scheme (NPS). The District Judiciary employees appointed against the posts or vacancies advertised for recruitment prior to the issuance of SR0-400 dated December 24 2009, introducing the NPS, and are covered under the NPS upon joining service on or after January 1, 2010, shall be entitled to exercise a one-time option for coverage under the OPS, according to an order issued by Haq Nawaz Khan Principal Secretary to Chief Justice. The order issued in keeping with the direction of the Chief Justice underscores that the option shall be exercised by the concerned eligible District Judiciary employee within the stipulated period of three weeks, that is up to October 30, 2026 from its issuance date. The order further emphasises that the eligible employee shall exercise the option for coverage under the OPS by submitting the duly completed form along with the requisite supporting documents, to the concerned Drawing and Disbursing Officer (DDO)/ Presiding Officer. District Judiciary employees who are eligible to exercise the option, but do not exercise the same within the stipulated time, shall continue to be covered by the NPS. The order indicates that upon receipt of the option forms, along with the requisite supporting documents, from eligible employees, the concerned DDO/Presiding Officer shall verify and certify the forms, prepare a list of employees who have exercised the option, and forward these to the Chief Justice Secretariat through the concerned Principal District and Sessions Judge, on or before November 12, 2026. The Chief Administrative Officer/Accounts Officer/S.O. (Administration), as the case may be, shall also prepare a consolidated list of eligible employees of the district who have exercised the option and forward the same to this Secretariat for cross-verification, it says. Upon receipt of the option forms seeking coverage under the OPS, the Secretariat shall scrutinise each case and determine the eligibility of the applicant in accordance with the instructions contained in the related Government Order and issue appropriate orders accordingly. On issuance of the requisite order(s) by this Secretariat, the concerned DDO/Presiding Officer shall initiate the process for closure of the NPS account(s) of the employee(s) concerned through the respective Treasury Officer and undertake such further action as may be required under the Government order. The Government of Jammu and Kashmir, vide SR0-400 dated December 24, 2009, introduced the Defined Contribution Pension Scheme (New Pension Scheme) in place of the Defined Benefit Pension Scheme (Old Pension Scheme) for all Government employees appointed or brought on the regular establishment on or after January 1, 201 0. The said Scheme became applicable to the staff of the District Judiciary by virtue of Rule 14 of the Jammu and Kashmir Ministerial and Other Staff of the Subordinate Courts (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 2016, the order said. The High Court has now extended the benefit of the OPS to the District Judiciary employees in pursuance of the order ( No. 305F of 2026 dated September 28, 2026, issued by the Finance Department (Codes Department), which has introduced a one-time option for coverage under the Defined Benefit Pension Scheme (Old Pension Scheme) for those Government employees who were appointed against posts for which recruitment had been advertised prior to the issuance of the notification introducing NPS vide SR0-400 dated December 24, 2009, and are covered under the NPS upon joining service on or after January 1, 2010.

stories.headline: PDP: The “cry baby” of Kashmir Politics
stories.title: PDP: The “cry baby” of Kashmir Politics
stories.summary: The Peoples Democratic Party entered the political landscape of Jammu and Kashmir with the promise of providing an alternative political narrative. It projected itself as a party capable of challenging the traditional dominance of the National Conference and claimed to represent a softer, more responsive and people-oriented politics. Over the years, however, the PDP has increasingly transformed itself from a party seeking to shape political events into one perpetually complaining about them. Its political vocabulary today appears dominated by grievance, victimhood and accusations against almost every other political force. In that sense, the PDP increasingly resembles the “cry baby” of Kashmir politics—a party that finds reasons to complain about developments but struggles to offer a convincing political roadmap of its own. The PDP was created in 1999 under the leadership of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed and quickly occupied an important space in Kashmir politics. It challenged the National Conference at a time when the latter had long dominated the Valley's electoral landscape. Its promise of a “healing touch” appealed to sections of society looking for an alternative. After the 2002 Assembly elections, the PDP became part of the coalition government with Congress, and Mufti Mohammad Sayeed became Chief Minister under a rotational arrangement. The party had arrived as a serious political force. The difficulty for the PDP has been reconciling its rhetoric with its record in government. While in opposition, it frequently adopted an aggressive posture against those exercising power. Once in government, however, it was itself required to function within the same constitutional and administrative system it had criticised. This contradiction became particularly visible after the 2014 Assembly elections. The PDP had fought the 2014 election largely by presenting itself as a political barrier against the BJP's expansion into Jammu and Kashmir. Yet, after the election produced a fractured mandate, the PDP entered into an alliance with the BJP and formed the government. The alliance may have been justified at the time as an attempt to reconcile the electoral mandates of Jammu and Kashmir, but politically it exposed the enormous distance between the PDP's electoral rhetoric and its willingness to exercise power with the very party it had opposed. The BJP's ideological position was hardly a secret. Its views on Article 370, nationalism and the constitutional integration of Jammu and Kashmir had been publicly articulated for decades. The PDP nevertheless chose to share governmental responsibility with it. That historical fact makes some of the PDP's later political rhetoric difficult to separate from its own record. The death of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed in January 2016 was a turning point. Mehbooba Mufti eventually became Chief Minister and inherited not only the government but also the contradictions of the coalition. The unrest following the killing of Hizbul Mujahideen commander Burhan Wani in July 2016 created one of the most difficult periods of her tenure. As Chief Minister, Mehbooba Mufti had responsibility for maintaining law and order and defending governmental action. Her language as head of government was naturally very different from the language the PDP would subsequently employ from opposition. That contrast illustrates the central problem confronting the party. When exercising power, it has defended the compulsions of governance; when out of power, it frequently portrays similar governmental compulsions as evidence of injustice. A political party is entitled to change its position when circumstances change, but repeated shifts inevitably invite questions about consistency. The collapse of the PDP-BJP coalition in 2018 pushed the PDP into a political crisis from which it has struggled to recover fully. The constitutional changes of August 5, 2019 fundamentally altered Jammu and Kashmir's political environment. Article 370 was rendered inoperative in its earlier form, Article 35A ceased to operate, and the former State was reorganised into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The PDP responded by placing these developments at the centre of its political narrative. Opposition to the August 2019 changes is a legitimate political position within democratic discourse, and the party is entitled to advocate its constitutional viewpoint. But a political organisation ultimately has to tell people not merely what it opposes but what it proposes to accomplish under existing circumstances. This is where the PDP's present difficulty becomes visible. Its politics increasingly appears centred around a catalogue of grievances—Article 370, detention of political leaders and other persons, relations with the Centre, security measures, administrative decisions, the functioning of the elected government and the political positions of rival parties. On almost every major issue, the PDP presents itself as the aggrieved party. When the Centre acts, PDP complains. When the National Conference acts, PDP complains. When political space shifts towards another party, PDP complains. When its leaders leave, the party portrays itself as the victim of circumstances. When other parties appropriate issues once identified with PDP, it again complains of political betrayal or inconsistency. Politics, however, cannot permanently operate on grievance. A political party has to create hope, provide solutions and persuade people that it possesses a credible programme for the future. The younger generation of Kashmir is increasingly concerned about employment, education, entrepreneurship, tourism, technology, infrastructure and opportunities in the wider Indian and global economy. Constitutional and political questions remain important, but they cannot be the sole content of politics indefinitely. The PDP also faces a fundamental contradiction in its relationship with the National Conference. For years, it sought to distinguish itself from the NC. The PDP offered “self-rule”; the NC traditionally advocated autonomy. The PDP claimed to represent a different political approach and repeatedly attacked the Abdullah-led party for its historical record. Yet today the political space separating the two parties has narrowed considerably on several major issues. Both criticise the constitutional changes of August 2019. Both speak about restoration of constitutional protections, though their formulations and political strategies differ. Both compete for substantially overlapping segments of the electorate in Kashmir. The result is an identity problem for the PDP. If it takes positions similar to the National Conference, voters may ask why they need the PDP when the NC possesses a larger organisation and a longer political history. If it moves further towards sharper rhetoric merely to distinguish itself, it risks restricting its ability to expand beyond a particular political constituency. This dilemma has contributed to the politics of constant complaint. Instead of defining an entirely new political agenda, PDP frequently reacts to what the NC, BJP or Central Government is doing. Reactive politics may keep a party visible in newspapers and television debates, but visibility is not the same thing as political revival. The 2024 Jammu and Kashmir Assembly election demonstrated the scale of the challenge. The National Conference emerged as the dominant force in the Valley, while the PDP's representation was sharply reduced compared with the position it once occupied. That electoral result cannot simply be explained away by circumstances. It represented a message from voters that the PDP needed serious political introspection. The party has nevertheless shown that it retains pockets of political relevance. Its later success in the Budgam Assembly by-election demonstrated that political space in Kashmir remains fluid and that no party can permanently take voters for granted. But an isolated electoral revival cannot substitute for rebuilding a broad political organisation and developing a coherent long-term programme. The PDP must also confront the consequences of its own political history. It cannot erase the years during which it exercised power. It cannot speak as though every controversial decision in Jammu and Kashmir was taken by somebody else. Governments headed by the PDP faced protests, security challenges, administrative controversies and difficult political decisions. Political accountability does not disappear merely because a party moves from treasury benches to opposition benches. That is precisely why perpetual victimhood becomes politically unconvincing. A mature political party accepts responsibility for its own record while criticising its opponents. It explains what it did right, acknowledges what went wrong and tells voters what it would do differently in the future. Constantly locating responsibility elsewhere may provide immediate political convenience, but it does not necessarily rebuild credibility. Kashmir itself is changing. A new generation has emerged that did not experience many of the political events which shaped the leadership of older parties in the same way. Its aspirations are increasingly connected with education, economic mobility, technology, entrepreneurship, employment and access to opportunities beyond Jammu and Kashmir. Any party seeking a durable future must speak to these aspirations. The PDP therefore faces a choice. It can continue to define itself principally through grievances—against New Delhi, against BJP, against NC, against administrative decisions and against changing political circumstances—or it can rediscover the reformist political energy with which it originally entered Kashmir politics. A party that once challenged the established political order cannot indefinitely survive by complaining that the political order has changed against it. The description of PDP as the “cry baby” of Kashmir politics is therefore not merely a rhetorical expression. It reflects a deeper political criticism: the transition of a once agenda-setting party into an increasingly reactive political organisation. Kashmir does not need political parties competing over who can articulate the greatest grievance. It needs political organisations capable of offering competing visions of development, governance, employment, peace and democratic participation. The PDP has every democratic right to oppose policies with which it disagrees. It has every right to campaign for its constitutional positions and criticise both the Government of India and the elected government in Jammu and Kashmir. opening: The Peoples Democratic Party entered the political landscape of Jammu and Kashmir with the promise of providing an alternative political narrative.
It projected itself as a party capable of challenging the traditional dominance of the National Conference and claimed to represent a softer, more responsive and people-oriented politics.
body: Over the years, however, the PDP has increasingly transformed itself from a party seeking to shape political events into one perpetually complaining about them.
Its political vocabulary today appears dominated by grievance, victimhood and accusations against almost every other political force.

In that sense, the PDP increasingly resembles the “cry baby” of Kashmir politics—a party that finds reasons to complain about developments but struggles to offer a convincing political roadmap of its own.
The PDP was created in 1999 under the leadership of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed and quickly occupied an important space in Kashmir politics.
It challenged the National Conference at a time when the latter had long dominated the Valley's electoral landscape.
Its promise of a “healing touch” appealed to sections of society looking for an alternative.
After the 2002 Assembly elections, the PDP became part of the coalition government with Congress, and Mufti Mohammad Sayeed became Chief Minister under a rotational arrangement.
The party had arrived as a serious political force.
The difficulty for the PDP has been reconciling its rhetoric with its record in government.
While in opposition, it frequently adopted an aggressive posture against those exercising power.
Once in government, however, it was itself required to function within the same constitutional and administrative system it had criticised.
This contradiction became particularly visible after the 2014 Assembly elections.
The PDP had fought the 2014 election largely by presenting itself as a political barrier against the BJP's expansion into Jammu and Kashmir.
Yet, after the election produced a fractured mandate, the PDP entered into an alliance with the BJP and formed the government.

The alliance may have been justified at the time as an attempt to reconcile the electoral mandates of Jammu and Kashmir, but politically it exposed the enormous distance between the PDP's electoral rhetoric and its willingness to exercise power with the very party it had opposed.
The BJP's ideological position was hardly a secret.
Its views on Article 370, nationalism and the constitutional integration of Jammu and Kashmir had been publicly articulated for decades.
The PDP nevertheless chose to share governmental responsibility with it.
That historical fact makes some of the PDP's later political rhetoric difficult to separate from its own record.
The death of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed in January 2016 was a turning point.
Mehbooba Mufti eventually became Chief Minister and inherited not only the government but also the contradictions of the coalition.
The unrest following the killing of Hizbul Mujahideen commander Burhan Wani in July 2016 created one of the most difficult periods of her tenure.
As Chief Minister, Mehbooba Mufti had responsibility for maintaining law and order and defending governmental action.
Her language as head of government was naturally very different from the language the PDP would subsequently employ from opposition.
That contrast illustrates the central problem confronting the party.
When exercising power, it has defended the compulsions of governance; when out of power, it frequently portrays similar governmental compulsions as evidence of injustice.
A political party is entitled to change its position when circumstances change, but repeated shifts inevitably invite questions about consistency.
The collapse of the PDP-BJP coalition in 2018 pushed the PDP into a political crisis from which it has struggled to recover fully.
The constitutional changes of August 5, 2019 fundamentally altered Jammu and Kashmir's political environment.
Article 370 was rendered inoperative in its earlier form, Article 35A ceased to operate, and the former State was reorganised into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
The PDP responded by placing these developments at the centre of its political narrative.
Opposition to the August 2019 changes is a legitimate political position within democratic discourse, and the party is entitled to advocate its constitutional viewpoint.
But a political organisation ultimately has to tell people not merely what it opposes but what it proposes to accomplish under existing circumstances.
This is where the PDP's present difficulty becomes visible.

Its politics increasingly appears centred around a catalogue of grievances—Article 370, detention of political leaders and other persons, relations with the Centre, security measures, administrative decisions, the functioning of the elected government and the political positions of rival parties.
On almost every major issue, the PDP presents itself as the aggrieved party.
When the Centre acts, PDP complains.
When the National Conference acts, PDP complains.
When political space shifts towards another party, PDP complains.
When its leaders leave, the party portrays itself as the victim of circumstances.
When other parties appropriate issues once identified with PDP, it again complains of political betrayal or inconsistency.
Politics, however, cannot permanently operate on grievance.
A political party has to create hope, provide solutions and persuade people that it possesses a credible programme for the future.

The younger generation of Kashmir is increasingly concerned about employment, education, entrepreneurship, tourism, technology, infrastructure and opportunities in the wider Indian and global economy.
Constitutional and political questions remain important, but they cannot be the sole content of politics indefinitely.
The PDP also faces a fundamental contradiction in its relationship with the National Conference.
For years, it sought to distinguish itself from the NC.
The PDP offered “self-rule”; the NC traditionally advocated autonomy.
The PDP claimed to represent a different political approach and repeatedly attacked the Abdullah-led party for its historical record.
Yet today the political space separating the two parties has narrowed considerably on several major issues.
Both criticise the constitutional changes of August 2019.
Both speak about restoration of constitutional protections, though their formulations and political strategies differ.
Both compete for substantially overlapping segments of the electorate in Kashmir.
The result is an identity problem for the PDP.
If it takes positions similar to the National Conference, voters may ask why they need the PDP when the NC possesses a larger organisation and a longer political history.
If it moves further towards sharper rhetoric merely to distinguish itself, it risks restricting its ability to expand beyond a particular political constituency.
This dilemma has contributed to the politics of constant complaint.
Instead of defining an entirely new political agenda, PDP frequently reacts to what the NC, BJP or Central Government is doing.
Reactive politics may keep a party visible in newspapers and television debates, but visibility is not the same thing as political revival.
The 2024 Jammu and Kashmir Assembly election demonstrated the scale of the challenge.
The National Conference emerged as the dominant force in the Valley, while the PDP's representation was sharply reduced compared with the position it once occupied.
That electoral result cannot simply be explained away by circumstances.
It represented a message from voters that the PDP needed serious political introspection.
The party has nevertheless shown that it retains pockets of political relevance.
Its later success in the Budgam Assembly by-election demonstrated that political space in Kashmir remains fluid and that no party can permanently take voters for granted.
But an isolated electoral revival cannot substitute for rebuilding a broad political organisation and developing a coherent long-term programme.
The PDP must also confront the consequences of its own political history.
It cannot erase the years during which it exercised power.
It cannot speak as though every controversial decision in Jammu and Kashmir was taken by somebody else.
Governments headed by the PDP faced protests, security challenges, administrative controversies and difficult political decisions.
Political accountability does not disappear merely because a party moves from treasury benches to opposition benches.
That is precisely why perpetual victimhood becomes politically unconvincing.
A mature political party accepts responsibility for its own record while criticising its opponents.
It explains what it did right, acknowledges what went wrong and tells voters what it would do differently in the future.
Constantly locating responsibility elsewhere may provide immediate political convenience, but it does not necessarily rebuild credibility.
Kashmir itself is changing.
A new generation has emerged that did not experience many of the political events which shaped the leadership of older parties in the same way.
Its aspirations are increasingly connected with education, economic mobility, technology, entrepreneurship, employment and access to opportunities beyond Jammu and Kashmir.
Any party seeking a durable future must speak to these aspirations.
The PDP therefore faces a choice.

It can continue to define itself principally through grievances—against New Delhi, against BJP, against NC, against administrative decisions and against changing political circumstances—or it can rediscover the reformist political energy with which it originally entered Kashmir politics.
A party that once challenged the established political order cannot indefinitely survive by complaining that the political order has changed against it.
The description of PDP as the “cry baby” of Kashmir politics is therefore not merely a rhetorical expression.
It reflects a deeper political criticism: the transition of a once agenda-setting party into an increasingly reactive political organisation.
Kashmir does not need political parties competing over who can articulate the greatest grievance.
It needs political organisations capable of offering competing visions of development, governance, employment, peace and democratic participation.
The PDP has every democratic right to oppose policies with which it disagrees.
It has every right to campaign for its constitutional positions and criticise both the Government of India and the elected government in Jammu and Kashmir.
But opposition acquires credibility when it is accompanied by an alternative.
The real challenge before PDP is therefore not to prove that it has reasons to complain.
Every opposition party can find reasons to complain.
Its challenge is to prove that it still has something new to offer.
Until it succeeds in doing so, the image of the PDP as the “cry baby of Kashmir politics” will remain a political criticism that the party will find increasingly difficult to answer.

stories.title: BJP stages protest outside Congress office in Jammu
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 10: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday held a protest demonstration outside the Congress office in Jammu, accusing the Leader of Opposition (LoP) in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and his other party colleagues of resorting to double standards. Led by J&K BJP vice presidents Priya Sethi (former minister) and Rekha Mahajan; general secretary Sanjita Dogra; Mahila Morcha president Neha Mahajan and other senior leaders, the protesters declared that India would not tolerate the insult or humiliation of women. J&K BJP president and Rajya Sabha MP Sat Sharma was prominent among those present. J&K BJP general secretaries Baldev Singh Billawaria and Gopal Mahajan, MLAs Dr Narinder Singh, CP Ganga, Dr Devinder Manyal, Vikram Randhawa, Prof Gharu Ram, Yudhvir Sethi, Arvind Gupta, Surinder Bhagat and Rajiv Bhagat, state office bearers, Morcha Presidents and other senior leaders were also present. Raising slogans against Congress, the demonstrators criticised the Congress leadership for, what they alleged, “practising double standards on women's dignity while using slogans such as “smashing the patriarchy” to mislead the public.” The protesters demanded Rahul Gandhi's resignation, holding him accountable for the conduct and politics of his party. Sat Sharma, addressing the demonstrators, said that Rahul Gandhi should resign, take responsibility for the conduct of his party and stop preaching about women's empowerment while serious questions were being raised about the behaviour of Congress leaders towards women. He asserted that the dignity of women could not be compromised for political convenience and that those who lectured the nation on women's rights must first demonstrate consistency through their own conduct. Sat Sharma criticised Rahul Gandhi and the Congress leadership alleging that their public claims of standing for women's rights contradicted the conduct attributed to Congress leaders. He said that allegations of misbehaviour towards female police personnel by Congress leaders and workers demanded serious accountability. He further accused Congress of pursuing a political agenda targetting national security agencies and undermining public confidence in constitutional institutions. Questioning Congress's silence over serious allegations against one of its MPs in a molestation case, Sat Sharma asked why Rahul Gandhi and other senior Congress leaders had not shown the same vocal concern for women's dignity in that matter. He stressed that women's respect was not a political slogan but a fundamental social responsibility and Rahul Gandhi must answer for his party's double standards and resign rather than evade accountability. Priya Sethi said that women's dignity must remain above partisan politics and that Congress must answer for the contradiction between its public messaging and the conduct it is accused of defending. Rekha Mahajan said that women deserved respect, security and equal dignity in every sphere of life, adding that political slogans could not substitute for accountability. Sanjita Dogra said that women expected sincerity and consistency from political leaders, not selective outrage on issues concerning their rights. Neha Mahajan said that BJP's women workers would continue to raise their voices against every instance of disrespect towards women and demand accountability from those holding public office.
